danish.title: Femtende bog (1812–13) — Kapitel 13
paragraphs: I det ydre havde Pierre næsten ikke forandret sig. I udseende var han, som han altid havde været. Som før var han adspredt og syntes optaget, ikke af det der var foran hans øjne, men af noget særligt, der tilhørte ham alene. Forskellen mellem hans tidligere og nuværende jeg var, at når han før ikke begreb det, der lå foran ham, eller blev sagt til ham, havde han smertefuldt rynket panden, som om han forgæves søgte at skelne noget i det fjerne. Nu glemte han stadig, hvad der blev sagt, og så stadig ikke, hvad der var foran ham, men han betragtede nu det, der var foran ham, med et knap mærkbart og tilsyneladende ironisk smil og lyttede til det sagte, skønt han tydeligvis så og hørte noget ganske andet. Før havde han virket som et godhjertet, men ulykkeligt menneske, og derfor havde folk været tilbøjelige til at undgå ham. Nu spillede et smil over livsglæden bestandigt om hans læber, og medfølelse med andre lyste i hans øjne med et spørgende blik, som ville han vide, om de var lige så tilfredse som han, og folk følte sig tilpas i hans nærhed.

Førhen havde han talt meget, blev ophidset, når han talte, og lyttede sjældent; nu lod han sig sjældent rive med i samtale og forstod at lytte på en sådan måde, at folk beredvilligt betroede ham deres mest intime hemmeligheder.

Fyrstinden, der aldrig havde kunnet lide Pierre og havde været ham særligt fjendtligt stemt, siden hun følte sig i gæld til ham efter den gamle greves død, begyndte nu efter et kort ophold i Orjol — hvor hun var kommet med den hensigt at vise Pierre, at hun trods hans utaknemmelighed betragtede det som sin pligt at passe ham — til sin egen overraskelse og ærgrelse at opdage, at hun var blevet glad for ham. Pierre søgte på ingen måde hendes anerkendelse; han studerede hende blot med interesse. Før havde hun følt, at han betragtede hende med ligegyldighed og ironi, og derfor havde hun trukket sig ind i sig selv, som hun plejede over for andre, og havde kun vist ham den kampberedte side af sin natur; men nu syntes han at forsøge at forstå de mest intime steder i hendes hjerte, og mistroisk i begyndelsen, men siden med taknemmelighed lod hun ham se de skjulte, venlige sider af sin karakter.

Den snedigste mand kunne ikke med større held have sneget sig ind i hendes fortrolighed, vakt minder om de bedste tider i hendes ungdom og vist medfølelse med dem. Alligevel bestod Pierres snedighed ganske enkelt i at finde glæde ved at lokke de menneskelige egenskaber frem hos den forbitrede, hårde og — på sin egen vis — stolte fyrstinde.
»Ja, han er et meget, meget venligt menneske, når han ikke er under indflydelse af slette mennesker, men af folk som mig,« tænkte hun.

Også hans tjenere — Terenti og Vaska — lagde på deres egen måde mærke til den forandring, der var sket med Pierre. De mente, at han var blevet meget »simplere«. Terenti stod ofte, når han havde hjulpet ham af med tøjet og ønsket ham godnat, med sin herres støvler i hænderne og tøj over armen for at se, om han ikke ville begynde en snak. Og Pierre standsede Terenti, når han lagde mærke til, at denne ønskede at snakke, og beholdt ham gerne.
»Nå, fortæl mig... hvordan fik du fat i mad?« spurgte han.

Og Terenti begyndte at fortælle om Moskvas ødelæggelse og om den gamle greve og stod længe med tøjet i hænderne og talte, eller somme tider lyttede til Pierres historier, og gik derpå ud i gangen med en behagelig følelse af fortrolighed med sin herre og hengivenhed for ham.

Den læge, der behandlede Pierre og besøgte ham hver dag, skønt han anså det for sin pligt som læge at posere som en mand, hvis hvert øjeblik var af værdi for den lidende menneskehed, sad i timevis sammen med Pierre og fortalte sine yndlingsanekdoter og sine iagttagelser om sine patienters karakter i almindelighed og kvindernes i særdeleshed.
»Det er en fornøjelse at tale med et menneske som ham; han er ikke som vores provinsbeboere,« sagde han.
Der var adskillige franske fanger i Orjol, og lægen bragte en af dem, en ung italiener, med på besøg hos Pierre.
Denne officer begyndte at aflægge Pierre besøg, og fyrstinden plejede at drille ham med den ømhed, italieneren udtrykte for ham.
Italieneren syntes kun lykkelig, når han kunne komme og besøge Pierre, tale med ham, fortælle om sin fortid, sit hjem og sin kærlighed og udøse sin harme over franskmændene og især over Napoleon.
»Hvis alle russere blot ligner Dem en smule, er det en helligbrøde at bekrige et sådant folk,« sagde han til Pierre. »De, som har lidt så meget under franskmændene, nærer ikke engang had mod dem.«
Pierre havde vakt italienerens lidenskabelige hengivenhed blot ved at lokke det bedste i hans natur frem og finde glæde heri.

I de sidste dage af Pierres ophold i Orjol kom hans gamle frimurerkammerat grev Willarski, der havde introduceret ham til logen i 1807, for at besøge ham. Willarski var gift med en russisk arving, der ejede et stort gods i Orjol-provinsen, og han beklædte en midlertidig stilling i intendanturafdelingen dér.

Da Willarski hørte, at Bezukhov var i Orjol, opsøgte han ham med de venskabserklæringer og den fortrolighed, som mennesker, der mødes i en ørken, gerne udviser. Willarski kedede sig i Orjol og var glad for at træffe en mand af sin egen kreds og, som han troede, med lignende interesser.
Men til sin overraskelse opdagede Willarski snart, at Pierre var sakket langt bagud tiden og var sunket, som han udtrykte det for sig selv, ned i apati og egoisme.
»Du lader dig gå, kære ven,« sagde han.

Men trods alt fandt Willarski det nu mere behageligt at være sammen med Pierre, end det havde været før, og kom for at besøge ham hver dag. For Pierre, mens han betragtede og lyttede til Willarski, var det underligt at tænke, at han selv for kort tid siden havde været sådan.

Willarski var en gift mand med familie, travlt optaget af familiens anliggender, hustruens anliggender og sine embedspligter. Han betragtede alle disse beskæftigelser som hindringer for livet og anså dem alle for foragtelige, fordi deres formål var hans egen og hans families velfærd. Militære, administrative, politiske og frimureranliggender optog bestandigt hans opmærksomhed. Og Pierre, uden at forsøge at ændre den andens synspunkter og uden at fordømme ham, men med det stille, glade og forundrede smil, der nu var blevet ham en vane, interesserede sig for dette mærkværdige, men højst velkendte fænomen.

Der var et nyt træk i Pierres forhold til Willarski, til fyrstinden, til lægen og til alle de mennesker, han nu mødte, som skaffede ham den almene velvilje. Det var hans anerkendelse af umuligheden af at ændre et menneskes overbevisninger med ord og hans erkendelse af muligheden for, at enhver tænker, føler og ser tingene fra sit eget synspunkt. Denne lovlige egenart hos hvert enkelt individ, som førhen havde ophidset og irriteret Pierre, var nu blevet grundlaget for den medfølelse, han nærede, og den interesse, han tog i andre mennesker. Forskellen, og somme tider den fuldstændige modsætning, mellem menneskers meninger og deres liv, og mellem den ene og den anden, glædede ham og aflokkede ham et morsomt og venligt smil.

I praktiske anliggender følte Pierre uventet et tyngdepunkt i sig, som han før havde savnet. Førhen havde alle pengesager — især anmodninger om penge, som han som en overmåde velhavende mand hyppigt blev udsat for — bragt ham i en tilstand af håbløs ophidselse og forvirring. »Skal jeg give eller ej?« havde han spurgt sig selv. »Jeg har, og han trænger. Men en anden trænger endnu mere. Hvem trænger mest? Og måske er de begge to svindlere?« I gamle dage havde han ikke kunnet finde en udvej af alle disse overvejelser og havde givet til alle, der bad, så længe han havde noget at give. Førhen havde han befundet sig i en lignende forvirring over ethvert spørgsmål vedrørende sin formue, når den ene rådede til ét og den anden til noget andet.

Nu opdagede han til sin overraskelse, at han ikke længere følte hverken tvivl eller forvirring i disse spørgsmål. Der var nu inden i ham en dommer, der efter en regel, han ikke selv kendte, afgjorde, hvad der burde og ikke burde gøres.

Han var lige så ligeglad med pengesager som hidtil, men nu følte han sig sikker på, hvad der burde og ikke burde gøres. Første gang han henvendte sig til sin nye dommer, var da en fransk fange, en oberst, opsøgte ham og efter at have talt længe om sine bedrifter sluttede med noget, der nærmest var et krav om, at Pierre skulle give ham fire tusind franc at sende til hans kone og børn. Pierre afslog uden den mindste vanskelighed eller anstrengelse og undrede sig bagefter over, hvor enkelt og let det havde været, hvad der før havde forekommet uoverkommeligt svært. Samtidig med at han afslog oberstens krav, besluttede han, at han måtte bruge list, når han forlod Orjol, for at formå den italienske officer til at modtage nogle penge, som han tydeligvis trængte til. Et yderligere bevis på Pierres mere afklarede syn på praktiske forhold var hans afgørelse vedrørende hans kones gæld og genopbygningen af hans huse i og nær Moskva.
Hans hovedforvalter kom til ham i Orjol, og Pierre regnede efter sammen med ham på sin formindskede indkomst. Moskvas brand havde kostet ham ifølge forvalterens beregning omkring to millioner rubler.

For at trøste Pierre over disse tab fremlagde hovedforvalteren et overslag, der viste, at hans indkomst trods tabene ikke ville blive formindsket, men endda forøget, hvis han nægtede at betale sin kones gæld, som han ikke var forpligtet til at indfri, og undlod at genopbygge sit hus i Moskva og landstedet på sit moskogods, der havde kostet ham firs tusind rubler om året uden at indbringe noget.
»Ja, ja, det er naturligvis rigtigt,« sagde Pierre med et muntert smil. »Jeg har slet ikke brug for alt det. Ved at blive ruineret er jeg blevet meget rigere.«

Men i januar kom Savjelitj (hans forvalter) fra Moskva og gav ham en beretning om tingenes tilstand dér og talte om et overslag, en arkitekt havde lavet over udgifterne til genopbygning af by- og landhuset, som om det var en afgjort sag. Samtidig modtog han breve fra fyrst Vasilij og andre petersborgske bekendte, der talte om hans kones gæld. Og Pierre besluttede, at forvalterens forslag, der havde glædet ham så meget, var forkerte, og at han måtte rejse til Petersborg for at ordne sin kones affærer og bygge op igen i Moskva. Hvorfor det var nødvendigt, vidste han ikke, men han vidste med sikkerhed, at det var nødvendigt. Hans indkomst ville blive reduceret med tre fjerdedele, men han følte, det måtte ske.
Willarski var på vej til Moskva, og de aftalte at rejse sammen.

Under hele sin rekonvalescens i Orjol havde Pierre oplevet en følelse af glæde, frihed og liv; men da han under rejsen befandt sig i den åbne verden og så hundredvis af nye ansigter, forstærkedes den følelse. Hele rejsen igennem følte han sig som en skoledreng på ferie. Alle — postvognens kusk, postmesteren, bønderne på vejene og i landsbyerne — havde en ny betydning for ham. Willarskis nærværelse og bemærkninger, der ustandselig beklagede Ruslands uvidenhed og fattigdom og dets tilbageståenhed i forhold til Europa, øgede kun Pierres glæde. Hvor Willarski så død og stilstand, så Pierre en usædvanlig styrke og vitalitet — den kraft, der i det vældige rum midt i sneen opretholdt dette oprindelige, ejendommelige og enestående folks liv. Han modsagde ikke Willarski og syntes endda at give ham ret — en tilsyneladende enighed var den enkleste måde at undgå diskussioner, der ikke førte nogen vegne — og han smilede glad, mens han lyttede til ham.

english.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: Outwardly, Pierre had barely changed at all. He looked the same as he always had. He was still absent-minded and seemed occupied not with what was in front of him but with something of his own. The difference between the old Pierre and the new was this: before, when he failed to grasp what was before him or what was being said, he would furrow his brow painfully, as if straining to make out something in the distance. Now he still forgot what people said to him and still didn't see what was right before his eyes, but he looked at everything with a barely perceptible, seemingly ironic smile, and listened to what was said while clearly seeing and hearing something entirely different. Before, he had seemed like a kindhearted but unhappy man, and people had tended to avoid him. Now a smile of pure joy played constantly around his lips, and his eyes shone with sympathy for others and a quiet question: were they as happy as he was? People felt genuinely pleased to be around him.

Before, he had talked a lot, got excited when he spoke, and rarely listened. Now he seldom got carried away in conversation and knew how to listen in a way that made people readily share their most intimate secrets with him.

The princess, who had never liked Pierre and had been especially hostile toward him since feeling indebted to him after the old count's death, had now—after staying a short time in Orel, where she had come intending to show Pierre that despite his ingratitude she felt duty-bound to nurse him—found to her surprise and irritation that she had grown fond of him. Pierre made no effort to win her approval; he simply studied her with interest. Before, she had felt that he looked at her with indifference and irony, so she had retreated into herself as she did with everyone, showing him only her combative side. But now he seemed to be reaching for the most hidden places in her heart, and—mistrustfully at first, then gratefully—she let him see the kind, gentle sides of her nature.

The most cunning person in the world couldn't have won her trust more effectively, drawing out memories of the best times of her youth and showing sympathy for them. Yet Pierre's cunning consisted simply in the pleasure he took in bringing out the human qualities of this bitter, hardened, and—in her own way—proud princess.
"Yes, he's a very, very kind man when he's not under the influence of bad people but of people like me," she thought.

His servants too—Terenty and Vaska—noticed the change in Pierre in their own way. They thought he had become much "simpler." Terenty, after helping him undress and wishing him good night, would often linger with his master's boots in his hands and clothes over his arm, hoping Pierre might start a conversation. And Pierre, noticing that Terenty wanted to chat, usually kept him there.
"Well, tell me—how did you manage to get food?" he would ask.

And Terenty would start talking about the destruction of Moscow and the old count, standing there a long time holding the clothes and talking, or sometimes listening to Pierre's stories, before going out to the hall with a pleasant feeling of closeness to his master and genuine affection for him.

The doctor who attended Pierre and visited him every day—though he felt obligated to act as if his every moment were precious to suffering humanity—would sit for hours with Pierre, telling his favorite stories and sharing observations about his patients' characters, especially the ladies.
"It's a pleasure to talk to a man like that; he's nothing like our provincial types," he would say.
There were several French prisoners of war in Orel, and the doctor brought one of them, a young Italian, to meet Pierre.
This officer began visiting Pierre regularly, and the princess liked to tease him about the Italian's open affection.
The Italian seemed happy only when he could visit Pierre, talk with him, tell him about his past life back home and his love, and pour out his outrage against the French and especially Napoleon.
"If all Russians are anything like you, it's a sin to fight such a nation," he told Pierre. "You, who suffered so much from the French, don't even feel any resentment toward them."
Pierre had won the Italian's passionate devotion simply by drawing out the best in him and taking pleasure in doing so.

During Pierre's last days in Orel, his old Masonic acquaintance Count Willarski—who had introduced him to the lodge back in 1807—came to see him. Willarski had married a Russian heiress with a large estate in Orel province and held a temporary post in the local commissariat department.

Hearing that Bezukhov was in Orel, Willarski—though they had never been close—came to him with the kind of warm declarations of friendship that people who meet in a desert tend to exchange. Willarski was bored in Orel and was glad to meet someone from his own circle who, he assumed, shared his interests.
But to his surprise, Willarski quickly noticed that Pierre had fallen far behind the times and had sunk, as he put it to himself, into apathy and self-absorption.
"You're letting yourself go, my dear fellow," he said.

But despite all that, Willarski found it more pleasant than before to spend time with Pierre, and came to see him every day. To Pierre, as he watched and listened to Willarski, it seemed strange to think that he himself had been just like that not so long ago.

Willarski was a married man with a family, busy with his family affairs, his wife's affairs, and his official duties. He saw all these occupations as obstacles to real life, and considered them contemptible because their aim was merely the welfare of himself and his family. Military, administrative, political, and Masonic concerns constantly consumed his attention. And Pierre, without trying to change his views or condemning him, but with the calm, joyful, and amused smile that was now habitual, watched this strange yet very familiar phenomenon with interest.

There was something new in Pierre's dealings with Willarski, with the princess, with the doctor, and with everyone he met—something that earned him universal goodwill. It was his acceptance of the impossibility of changing anyone's mind through words, and his recognition that everyone thinks, feels, and sees things from their own perspective. This natural uniqueness of each person, which used to excite and irritate Pierre, now became the basis for the sympathy he felt and the interest he took in other people. The differences—and sometimes outright contradictions—between what people believed and how they lived, and between one person and another, pleased him and drew from him an amused, gentle smile.

In practical matters, Pierre unexpectedly discovered a sense of inner balance he had never had before. Previously, all financial questions—especially requests for money, to which he was constantly exposed as an extremely wealthy man—had thrown him into a state of helpless anxiety and confusion. "Should I give or not?" he would ask himself. "I have it and he needs it. But someone else needs it more. Who needs it most? And maybe they're both frauds?" In the old days he had found no way out of such dilemmas and had given to everyone who asked, as long as he had anything left to give. He had been in a similar state of paralysis regarding every question about his property, when one adviser said one thing and another said the opposite.

Now, to his surprise, he found that he no longer felt any doubt or confusion about these things. There was now a judge inside him who, by some rule Pierre couldn't identify, decided what should and shouldn't be done.

He was as indifferent to money as ever, but now he felt certain about what was right and what wasn't. The first time he relied on this new inner judge was when a French prisoner, a colonel, came to him and—after talking at length about his military exploits—essentially demanded that Pierre give him four thousand francs to send to his wife and children. Pierre refused without the slightest difficulty or effort, and was amazed afterward at how simple and easy something had been that once seemed impossibly hard. At the same time that he refused the colonel, he decided he would need to find a tactful way, when leaving Orel, to get the Italian officer to accept some money he clearly needed. Another sign of Pierre's more settled practical judgment was his decision about his wife's debts and the rebuilding of his houses in and near Moscow.
His head steward came to see him in Orel, and Pierre went over his reduced income with him. According to the steward's calculations, the burning of Moscow had cost Pierre about two million rubles.

To comfort Pierre for these losses, the steward presented an estimate showing that despite everything, his income would actually increase—if he refused to pay his wife's debts, which he was under no legal obligation to pay, and didn't rebuild his Moscow house or the country estate nearby, which had cost eighty thousand rubles a year and brought in nothing.
"Yes, of course, that's true," Pierre said with a cheerful smile. "I don't need any of that at all. By being ruined, I've become much richer."

But in January, Savelich arrived from Moscow with an account of the situation there, including an architect's estimate for rebuilding the town house and country house, speaking of it as a settled matter. Around the same time, Pierre received letters from Prince Vasili and other Petersburg acquaintances about his wife's debts. And Pierre decided that the steward's proposals, which had pleased him so much, were wrong—that he needed to go to Petersburg to settle his wife's affairs, and he needed to rebuild in Moscow. Why this was necessary he couldn't say, but he knew with certainty that it had to be done. His income would be cut by three-quarters, but he felt it was right.
Willarski was heading to Moscow, and they agreed to travel together.

Throughout his recovery in Orel, Pierre had felt a sense of joy, freedom, and life; but during his journey, surrounded by the open world and hundreds of new faces, that feeling only intensified. He felt like a schoolboy on holiday. Everyone—the coach driver, the post-house overseers, the peasants on the roads and in the villages—held a fresh significance for him. Willarski's constant complaints about the ignorance and poverty of Russia and its backwardness compared to Europe only heightened Pierre's delight. Where Willarski saw stagnation, Pierre saw extraordinary strength and vitality—the strength that sustained the life of this original, distinctive, and unique people across those vast, snow-covered spaces. He didn't argue with Willarski and even seemed to agree with him—since apparent agreement was the simplest way to avoid pointless debates—and he smiled joyfully as he listened.
